screens.title: Auditing and Logging for Security Compliance
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will build a practical understanding of how auditd and rsyslog work together to deliver trustworthy, compliant logging. You will learn why kernel-level auditing captures system calls and file access while rsyslog centralizes application and system messages. That combination lets you detect suspicious activity, support forensic timelines, and meet regulatory retention and integrity requirements. We will walk through writing precise auditd rules, loading them safely, searching events with ausearch, producing summaries with aureport, and configuring secure rsyslog forwarding using TLS. You will also see the common operational pitfalls — such as overly broad rules or missing log rotation — and how to avoid them. By the end you will be able to outline a secure logging architecture, implement targeted audit rules, and validate that events arrive at a remote log server in a way that preserves integrity and timestamps. Think about where your organization stores privileged activity logs, and whether those logs could be altered by an attacker — that question will guide design choices during the lesson.

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Accurate, protected logs are the backbone of incident response and regulatory proof. Auditd provides detailed host-level events, rsyslog enables centralized and secure collection.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.7 › Overview
In this lesson
Design a secure, auditable logging pipeline with auditd and rsyslog

We start with a conceptual view of roles: auditd captures kernel-level security events, while rsyslog aggregates application and system logs. Together they enable immutable event records and centralized analysis required by compliance frameworks.

Auditd
Kernel-level events, system calls, file access. Writes to /var/log/audit/audit.log.
Rsyslog
Central collector and forwarder. Use TLS for secure transport to a remote server.
What you will do
Write rules, trigger events, search logs, and enable TLS forwarding.
Starter tasks
  • Create targeted auditd rules for passwd and sudo activity.
  • Search the audit log using ausearch and summarize with aureport.
  • Configure rsyslog client to forward authpriv logs with TLS.
Why it matters
Proper auditing enables investigations and provides evidence required by compliance regulations.
Explore Key Topics
Audit rules, log analysis, and secure forwarding are the three pillars you will practice.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: In this first objectives slide I will outline four practical skills you'll acquire and why they matter in production. First, you will configure auditd rules that monitor specific system calls, file access, and user actions. This skill matters because precise rules reduce noise and provide the exact events investigators need. Second, you'll learn to analyze audit. log entries using ausearch and create reports with aureport. Knowing how to filter and summarize events rapidly saves time during an incident and helps you meet review requirements. Third, you'll configure rsyslog for centralized log collection and secure log transport using TLS. Centralizing logs prevents local tampering and equips you to scale monitoring across many hosts. Finally, we'll cover log rotation and secure storage, including retention policies required by compliance frameworks. Rotating and protecting logs prevents disk exhaustion and preserves evidence integrity. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you can verify your implementation in a lab or production-like environment.

screens.title: What is auditd and what does it record?
screens.narratorSegment: Auditd is the Linux Auditing System that captures kernel-level security events and writes them into an append-only audit log. As an architect you should understand that auditd hooks into syscall paths and filesystem watches to record actions like file reads, writes, attribute changes, executed commands, and authentication events. The daemon receives events from the kernel and stores them under a consistent location, commonly /var/log/audit/audit. log, which becomes the authoritative record for host activity. A concrete example is monitoring modifications to the password file: by attaching a watch on that file with the appropriate permissions flags you will see attempts to write or change attributes, and each event includes metadata such as the calling process, effective user ID, and timestamp. A common misconception is that auditd replaces traditional syslog; it does not. Auditd focuses on security-relevant kernel events, while syslog collects application and service messages. Another misconception is believing that more rules are always better — overly broad rules create high volume and can obscure important events and fill storage. Key takeaway: auditd gives you high-fidelity event data for security investigations, but you must design rules that are targeted, efficient, and verifiable.

keyIdea.title: Auditd defined
keyIdea.text: A kernel-level auditing framework that records security-relevant system events to a central audit log file for forensic and compliance use.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.7 › auditd Basics
Definition

Auditd captures syscall and file access events at the kernel level and writes them to an authoritative audit log. Events include who did what, when, and with which process context.

Example
A watch on /etc/passwd will create events when processes attempt to write or change file attributes, recording UID, PID, and timestamps.
Misconception
Auditd does not replace syslog. It complements syslog by providing kernel-level security data.
Key Takeaway

Use auditd for high-fidelity security events; keep rules targeted to avoid noise.

Annotated event fields
  • Timestamp and event type (audit record types)
  • Record metadata: PID, UID, EUID, AUid
  • System call or watched path and permission flags
  • Custom key for grouping related events
Practical check
Ensure /var/log/audit exists on immutable or well-monitored storage and verify auditd is running and receiving kernel events.

screens.title: Audit rule syntax and filters
screens.narratorSegment: Audit rules determine which events auditd records. The chapter gives two common syntaxes: file watches using a dash W flag and syscall rules using -a, -S, and field filters. Key elements to remember are the watch path, permission flags, and the custom key name that lets you group events for searches. For syscall rules, include architecture filters and field matches like UID or success flags to limit recorded events. A concrete pattern you will use often is watching critical files with write and attribute change permissions, which gives you notifications when those files are modified. Another frequent pattern is monitoring execve system calls for root or privileged users to capture command execution. A common mistake is adding broad syscall rules without field filters; that produces very high volumes and may miss the signal in the noise. When designing rules, think about the question you want the log to answer: who changed the file, which process did it, and was the action successful? Use the chapter's syntax elements as building blocks and test rules by triggering events and verifying with ausearch. That testing step ensures the rule behaves as intended.

keyIdea.title: Rule building blocks
keyIdea.text: Use watches for files and syscall rules with field filters; always attach a key for searchable grouping and test rules in a safe environment.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.7 › Rule Syntax
Rule patterns
Two core patterns: file watches with -w and syscall rules with -a and -S. Combine permissions, arch, uid filters and a key.
-w /etc/passwd -p wa -k passwd_changes
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S execve -F euid=0 -k root_commands
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S open -F success=0 -k failed_writes
Note: Use a custom key to make searches simpler and limit syscall rules by arch and uid filters.
Practical guidance
  • Prefer targeted watches for sensitive files over broad syscall coverage.
  • Include success or failure filters when you care about outcome.
  • Attach distinct keys for rule classes to ease ausearch queries.
Check your understanding
What key would you use to find all passwd change events? Answer: the key you set, for example passwd_changes.

screens.title: Example auditd rules — practical walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a practical example from the chapter: monitoring modifications to passwd and tracking sudo execution. The recipe is to create a rules file under the rules. d directory and then load it. The example rules watch the password and shadow files for write and attribute changes, and audit execve calls filtered to the sudo binary. After creating the rule file, you run the rules loader to apply them. To validate, perform a harmless action that triggers a rule, such as touching the passwd file with elevated privileges, then search the audit log using the custom keys. One useful pattern is to separate rule files by purpose and name them with a prefix so automation picks them up predictably. A misconception is to expect immediate human-friendly output; audit logs are raw and require ausearch or aureport to interpret. Another pitfall is not considering architecture filters on diverse fleets; include arch=b64 or arch=b32 where appropriate to avoid missing events. That testing cycle — write, load, trigger, search — is essential and will be repeated throughout the lab portion of this lesson.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.7 › Rule Walkthrough
Starter rules (file)
# Monitor all write access to /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow
-w /etc/passwd -p wa -k passwd_changes
-w /etc/shadow -p wa -k shadow_changes

# Monitor execve for sudo
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S execve -F path=/usr/bin/sudo -k sudo_exec
Save the file to /etc/audit/rules.d/99-custom.rules and run the loader to apply changes.
Validation steps
  1. Create the rule file and save it under rules.d.
  2. Run the rules loader command to apply rules.
  3. Trigger events such as a touch or a sudo command.
  4. Use ausearch with the key to find matching events.
Common mistake
Avoid creating overly broad syscall rules without filters; they will flood audit logs.

screens.title: Loading rules and operational pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: After you author audit rules, the operational cycle is load, validate, monitor, and refine. Use the loader tool to read rules from rules. d and apply them to the kernel. A common operational pitfall is making rule changes directly with temporary tools without persisting them to the rules. d directory, causing configuration drift after a reboot. Another problem is failing to plan for log volume: broad rules can quickly fill disk space, cause performance issues, or trigger automated processes to delete logs prematurely. For steady-state monitoring, define alert thresholds and dashboards that highlight spikes in specific keys or syscall types. Also, integrate log rotation and off-host forwarding so local storage is not the only copy. When you test, record timestamps and verify with system time synchronization so events across multiple hosts can be correlated. Finally, maintain separate rule files for different purposes — for example, authentication rules versus file integrity watches — and use clear keys so searches and reports are easy to run. The goal is an auditable, maintainable rule set that produces evidence without overwhelming operators. Loading rules and operational pitfalls means persist rules under rules.d, test changes, plan for volume, and integrate forwarding and rotation for resiliency.. In practical terms, from editing rules to steady-state monitoring. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.7 › Operational Pitfalls
Load & persist
Always place rule files under /etc/audit/rules.d and use the loader to apply them. This ensures rules survive restarts and are managed via configuration tools.
Checklist
  • Save rules to rules.d with clear names
  • Run the loader after editing
  • Validate events with ausearch
Avoiding volume problems
Design rules with filters and keys, and plan log rotation and remote forwarding. Monitor disk usage and set alerts to prevent full volumes.
Pro tip
Start with a small rule set in production, measure event rates, then expand carefully — this prevents surprises.

screens.title: Searching audit logs with ausearch
screens.narratorSegment: ausearch is the investigator's primary tool for filtering the raw audit log. It accepts keys, event types, message selectors, and more to produce a focused set of records for review. A typical use is searching by key, which returns only events that were tagged with that key when the rule fired. For example, if you created a key for passwd changes you can run a search with that key to extract only relevant events. ausearch also supports searching by event message or type — such as authentication events — and by field filters like user ID or success flags. One misconception is thinking ausearch produces human-friendly summaries; it returns raw audit records that still need interpretation. For quick overviews, use aureport. In practice, your workflow will be: trigger an action, run ausearch keyed to the rule, inspect the returned records to see process IDs and arguments, and then follow up with context searches if needed. Mastering ausearch patterns reduces investigation time and is essential during incident response. Searching audit logs with ausearch means a command-line search tool for extracting auditd records by key, type, and field filters to support investigations.. In practical terms, finding events quickly with keys, types, and filters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: A command-line search tool for extracting auditd records by key, type, and field filters to support investigations.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.7 › ausearch
Common search patterns
# Search by key
ausearch -k passwd_changes

# Search for failed authentication
ausearch -m USER_AUTH -sv no
Use keys as your primary search handle. Combine multiple filters for precise results.
Reading results
ausearch returns low-level records. Look for the audit message type, PID, UID, and syscall-specific fields to reconstruct the action.
Misconception
ausearch is not a reporting tool. Use it to find raw events, then summarize with aureport if you need aggregated metrics.

screens.title: Summarizing events with aureport
screens.narratorSegment: aureport is designed to convert raw audit records into digestible summaries that answer questions like: how many failures occurred today, which users ran privileged commands, or which hosts generated the most events. Use the time-range options to focus on a single day or a window, and the failed flag to isolate unsuccessful attempts. For example, you might run a daily summary that lists authentication failures and top users by event count, which helps operations detect trends. A useful workflow is to run aureport with a start-of-day timestamp and request a summary of failed events for rapid triage. Remember that aureport depends on the underlying audit log quality — if you have noisy or missing rules, reports will be unhelpful. A common mistake is over-relying on default reporting intervals; tune reports based on your operational needs, such as daily summaries for compliance or hourly checks for active incident windows. The practical benefit is turning low-level telemetry into management-ready metrics that can be archived for audits. Module 5 › Chapter 4.7 › aureport
Typical commands
# Summary for today
aureport --start today -ts 00:00:00 --end now --summary

# Show failed events
aureport -i --start today --failed
Use the interactive flag for more readable identifiers when available.
Operational use
Schedule regular reports for compliance windows and integrate their outputs into incident tickets when anomalies appear.
Pro tip
Combine aureport outputs with centralized log parsing to create dashboards for recurring audit metrics.

screens.title: Centralized logging with rsyslog
screens.narratorSegment: Rsyslog is an enterprise-grade system for collecting and forwarding logs from many sources. Centralized logging is required at scale because it prevents attackers from altering local logs and gives security teams a unified view across infrastructure. For an architect, the design choice is how and where to collect logs, how to secure transport, and how to store them to meet retention and integrity requirements. Rsyslog can forward messages over UDP or TCP, but for security you should use TLS on a dedicated port with certificate authentication. The chapter provides a client-side snippet to send all messages or to forward only specific facilities such as authentication messages. A practical example is forwarding authpriv entries to a remote collector for centralized authentication review. A frequent misconception is that centralization removes the need to protect local logs; it does not — local logs remain an important first line in incident handling. Key takeaway: centralize to preserve evidence and enable correlation, but secure both local and networked storage. Centralized logging with rsyslog means collect logs centrally to reduce tampering risk and enable multi-host correlation; protect transport and storage with tls and retention policies.. In practical terms, why centralization matters and how rsyslog fits into the design. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Client TLS snippet

$DefaultNetstreamDriverCAFile /etc/pki/tls/certs/ca.pem
$DefaultNetstreamDriverCertFile /etc/pki/tls/certs/client-cert.pem

screens.title: Log rotation, retention, and secure storage
screens.narratorSegment: Log rotation and secure storage are crucial operational controls. Rotation prevents disk full conditions and helps manage retention windows required by compliance frameworks. Use logrotate or equivalent to schedule rotations, compress archives, and remove older files according to policy. For compliance, you must implement retention periods — for example, a framework may require keeping logs for a defined number of months — and ensure logs are protected against tampering. Practical options include write-once media, append-only filesystems, or remote archival to an immutable store. A common mistake is rotating logs locally without ensuring a remote copy exists; this creates a single point of failure. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will build a practical understanding of how auditd and rsyslog work together to deliver trustworthy, compliant logging. You will learn why kernel-level auditing captures system calls and file access while rsyslog centralizes application and system messages. That combination lets you detect suspicious activity, support forensic timelines, and meet regulatory retention and integrity requirements. We will walk through writing precise auditd rules, loading them safely, searching events with ausearch, producing summaries with aureport, and configuring secure rsyslog forwarding using TLS. You will also see the common operational pitfalls — such as overly broad rules or missing log rotation — and how to avoid them. By the end you will be able to outline a secure logging architecture, implement targeted audit rules, and validate that events arrive at a remote log server in a way that preserves integrity and timestamps. Think about where your organization stores privileged activity logs, and whether those logs could be altered by an attacker — that question will guide design choices during the lesson.

In this first objectives slide I will outline four practical skills you'll acquire and why they matter in production. First, you will configure auditd rules that monitor specific system calls, file access, and user actions. This skill matters because precise rules reduce noise and provide the exact events investigators need. Second, you'll learn to analyze audit. log entries using ausearch and create reports with aureport. Knowing how to filter and summarize events rapidly saves time during an incident and helps you meet review requirements. Third, you'll configure rsyslog for centralized log collection and secure log transport using TLS. Centralizing logs prevents local tampering and equips you to scale monitoring across many hosts. Finally, we'll cover log rotation and secure storage, including retention policies required by compliance frameworks. Rotating and protecting logs prevents disk exhaustion and preserves evidence integrity. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you can verify your implementation in a lab or production-like environment.

On this second objectives slide we'll focus on verification, troubleshooting, and design choices an architect must make. You will practice testing auditd rules by performing controlled actions and confirming events with ausearch. That validation habit prevents gaps in coverage and helps tune rules to avoid log flooding. Next, you'll learn how to interpret aureport summaries and how to extract failed events or authentication failures. Being able to produce concise daily or weekly summaries is essential for operational reviews and audits. You'll also build the ability to create rsyslog client and server configurations that enforce TLS and certificate authentication; this protects logs from interception and tampering. Lastly, you will design retention and integrity measures such as immutable storage or write-once media, and coordinate time synchronization across hosts so timestamps are reliable. Each objective ends with a small test you can run locally — a touch, a sudo execution, a search, and a forward to a listening server — to prove competency. These are the operational checks that make your logging strategy trustworthy in production.

Auditd is the Linux Auditing System that captures kernel-level security events and writes them into an append-only audit log. As an architect you should understand that auditd hooks into syscall paths and filesystem watches to record actions like file reads, writes, attribute changes, executed commands, and authentication events. The daemon receives events from the kernel and stores them under a consistent location, commonly /var/log/audit/audit. log, which becomes the authoritative record for host activity. A concrete example is monitoring modifications to the password file: by attaching a watch on that file with the appropriate permissions flags you will see attempts to write or change attributes, and each event includes metadata such as the calling process, effective user ID, and timestamp. A common misconception is that auditd replaces traditional syslog; it does not. Auditd focuses on security-relevant kernel events, while syslog collects application and service messages. Another misconception is believing that more rules are always better — overly broad rules create high volume and can obscure important events and fill storage. Key takeaway: auditd gives you high-fidelity event data for security investigations, but you must design rules that are targeted, efficient, and verifiable.

Audit rules determine which events auditd records. The chapter gives two common syntaxes: file watches using a dash W flag and syscall rules using -a, -S, and field filters. Key elements to remember are the watch path, permission flags, and the custom key name that lets you group events for searches. For syscall rules, include architecture filters and field matches like UID or success flags to limit recorded events. A concrete pattern you will use often is watching critical files with write and attribute change permissions, which gives you notifications when those files are modified. Another frequent pattern is monitoring execve system calls for root or privileged users to capture command execution. A common mistake is adding broad syscall rules without field filters; that produces very high volumes and may miss the signal in the noise. When designing rules, think about the question you want the log to answer: who changed the file, which process did it, and was the action successful? Use the chapter's syntax elements as building blocks and test rules by triggering events and verifying with ausearch. That testing step ensures the rule behaves as intended.

Let's walk through a practical example from the chapter: monitoring modifications to passwd and tracking sudo execution. The recipe is to create a rules file under the rules. d directory and then load it. The example rules watch the password and shadow files for write and attribute changes, and audit execve calls filtered to the sudo binary. After creating the rule file, you run the rules loader to apply them. To validate, perform a harmless action that triggers a rule, such as touching the passwd file with elevated privileges, then search the audit log using the custom keys. One useful pattern is to separate rule files by purpose and name them with a prefix so automation picks them up predictably. A misconception is to expect immediate human-friendly output; audit logs are raw and require ausearch or aureport to interpret. Another pitfall is not considering architecture filters on diverse fleets; include arch=b64 or arch=b32 where appropriate to avoid missing events. That testing cycle — write, load, trigger, search — is essential and will be repeated throughout the lab portion of this lesson.

After you author audit rules, the operational cycle is load, validate, monitor, and refine. Use the loader tool to read rules from rules. d and apply them to the kernel. A common operational pitfall is making rule changes directly with temporary tools without persisting them to the rules. d directory, causing configuration drift after a reboot. Another problem is failing to plan for log volume: broad rules can quickly fill disk space, cause performance issues, or trigger automated processes to delete logs prematurely. For steady-state monitoring, define alert thresholds and dashboards that highlight spikes in specific keys or syscall types. Also, integrate log rotation and off-host forwarding so local storage is not the only copy. When you test, record timestamps and verify with system time synchronization so events across multiple hosts can be correlated. Finally, maintain separate rule files for different purposes — for example, authentication rules versus file integrity watches — and use clear keys so searches and reports are easy to run. The goal is an auditable, maintainable rule set that produces evidence without overwhelming operators. Loading rules and operational pitfalls means persist rules under rules.d, test changes, plan for volume, and integrate forwarding and rotation for resiliency.. In practical terms, from editing rules to steady-state monitoring. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

ausearch is the investigator's primary tool for filtering the raw audit log. It accepts keys, event types, message selectors, and more to produce a focused set of records for review. A typical use is searching by key, which returns only events that were tagged with that key when the rule fired. For example, if you created a key for passwd changes you can run a search with that key to extract only relevant events. ausearch also supports searching by event message or type — such as authentication events — and by field filters like user ID or success flags. One misconception is thinking ausearch produces human-friendly summaries; it returns raw audit records that still need interpretation. For quick overviews, use aureport. In practice, your workflow will be: trigger an action, run ausearch keyed to the rule, inspect the returned records to see process IDs and arguments, and then follow up with context searches if needed. Mastering ausearch patterns reduces investigation time and is essential during incident response. Searching audit logs with ausearch means a command-line search tool for extracting auditd records by key, type, and field filters to support investigations.. In practical terms, finding events quickly with keys, types, and filters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

aureport is designed to convert raw audit records into digestible summaries that answer questions like: how many failures occurred today, which users ran privileged commands, or which hosts generated the most events. Use the time-range options to focus on a single day or a window, and the failed flag to isolate unsuccessful attempts. For example, you might run a daily summary that lists authentication failures and top users by event count, which helps operations detect trends. A useful workflow is to run aureport with a start-of-day timestamp and request a summary of failed events for rapid triage. Remember that aureport depends on the underlying audit log quality — if you have noisy or missing rules, reports will be unhelpful. A common mistake is over-relying on default reporting intervals; tune reports based on your operational needs, such as daily summaries for compliance or hourly checks for active incident windows. The practical benefit is turning low-level telemetry into management-ready metrics that can be archived for audits. Summarizing events with aureport means converts audit logs into aggregated summaries for daily review, triage, and compliance reporting.. In practical terms, produce readable summaries and failed-event reports. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Rsyslog is an enterprise-grade system for collecting and forwarding logs from many sources. Centralized logging is required at scale because it prevents attackers from altering local logs and gives security teams a unified view across infrastructure. For an architect, the design choice is how and where to collect logs, how to secure transport, and how to store them to meet retention and integrity requirements. Rsyslog can forward messages over UDP or TCP, but for security you should use TLS on a dedicated port with certificate authentication.
